text:
The 49ers have a star-laden roster with all the names that have been around for a while.

Now, the organization needs a few new names to emerge and take their spots at the front of the class alongside Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey, George Kittle, Trent Williams, Nick Bosa and Fred Warner.

Most of the 49ers’ key roles are well-defined as the team reports to NFL training camp in Santa Clara on Saturday.

Here are the top competitions to watch as the 49ers point toward their regular-season opener against the Los Angeles Rams in Australia:

Left guard

The 49ers drafted guard Carver Willis in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, and he is likely to be involved in a competition for the job.

The team also signed Robert Jones, who started 17 games in 2024 with the Miami Dolphins before landing on injured reserve for the entire 2025 NFL season with a neck injury.

San Francisco 49ers

Find the latest San Francisco 49ers news, highlights, analysis and more with NBC Sports Bay Area and California.

But the slight front-runner as camp opens is second-year player Connor Colby.

Colby was a seventh-round draft pick last year. He had a good training camp to put himself in position to start six games when Ben Bartch was injured. Colby’s play plateaued, and eventually Spencer Burford took over as the starter.

Bartch signed with the Detroit Lions in the offseason, while Burford is now with the Las Vegas Raiders.

Colby has been in the system for more than a year, and he showed indications during the offseason program that his game has risen to a starter’s level.

Cornerback

Renardo Green did not face a competition last season for the starting job opposite of Deommodore Lenoir. That will change this summer.

The 49ers signed veteran Jack Jones, who started 33 games over the past two seasons with Las Vegas and the Miami Dolphins. He did not sign a one-year contract with the 49ers to settle for a backup job.

Green has been up and down during his first two seasons in the NFL. The 49ers selected him in the second round of the 2025 draft, and they expect a lot more from him.

“I think Renardo has done some really good things,” 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan said this offseason. “He’s played at a starter level, and I have much higher expectations for him than that.”

Edge rusher

Nick Bosa should be back after being sidelined in the third game of the 2025 season with a torn anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee.

If he can get back to double-digit sacks, that will be a huge boost for the 49ers after a season in which they totaled an NFL-low 20 sacks in 17 games.

But who is going to lock down the other edge in pass-rush situations?

That is why the 49ers selected Texas Tech defensive end Romello Height in the third round with the No. 70 overall pick.

Height had 6.5 sacks in his first five years of college football. Last season, surrounded by top talent on the Red Raiders’ line, he chalked up 10 sacks.

Height (6-foot-2, 239 pounds) must make an impact, but he has to earn his way onto the field.

The two players who topped the 49ers’ list in sacks, Clelin Ferrell and Bryce Huff, are not on the team. Ferrell remains unsigned and Huff opted for retirement. They had just four sacks apiece.

Sam Okuayinonu and Keion White are the top returners after registering just 3.0 and 1.5 sacks, respectively.

Wide receiver

The 49ers’ free-agent signing of Mike Evans takes care of one spot.

The other roles will be determined during training camp, as Ricky Peasall, Christian Kirk, Demarcus Robinson, De’Zhaun Stribling, Jordan Watkins, Jacob Cowing and others will be competing for significant playing time.

Cowing appears to be the front-runner to return to his 2024 role as the team’s primary punt returner. That would guarantee him one of the six spots reserved for wide receivers.

Pearsall must stay healthy. He appeared in 20 games over his first two NFL seasons. Last year, he was limited to just nine games due to a knee injury. His average of 58.7 yards receiving was tops among the wide receivers on the team.

Stribling showed early glimpses of why the 49ers liked him enough to select him with the No. 33 overall pick in the draft. He has good size, strength, speed, hands, route-running, toughness and blocking ability.

Robinson, Kirk and Watkins also showed plenty of attributes of their own during the offseason program.

Punter

The 49ers moved on from long-time NFL punter Thomas Morstead and signed Corliss Waitman as a free agent. Then, they added 27-year-old undrafted rookie Jack Bouwmeester to the roster.

Waitman spent the past two seasons with the Pittsburgh Steelers, where he had net punting averages of 41.9 and 41.8 yards.

Bouwmeester played his college football at Michigan State, Utah and Texas.

A native of Bendigo, Australia, Bouwmeester has an open door to win the job and be the 49ers’ punter when they open the regular season in Melbourne.

At the center are two anomalous developments – a nearly 55% increase in net income due to a surge in non-operating income and higher operational costs due to a combination of player acquisitions and departures.

All told, the Packers reported $132.5 million in net income for the fiscal year. They also reported $133.6 million in non-operating income from net investment gains, both local and national, and the NFL's sale of NFL Network to ESPN.

However, different within the annual financial picture is an operating loss of $1.1 million, which when subtracted from non-operating income results in the $132.5 million net income.

The primary reasons for the significant change in operational costs are as follows:

The Packers endured an uncommon year financially due to a combination of player acquisitions and departures. The structures of some new contracts, along with the required accounting of accelerated costs on released and traded players' deals, all hit the ledger in the same year, which accounted for the $131.7 million increase in player costs.

National revenue increased $20.6 million, or 4.8%, to a record $453.2 million, continuing the long-term growth and partnership the Packers have with the league.

The 2025 home schedule included only eight regular-season games, down from nine in 2024. Local revenue, which encompasses ticketing, sponsorships, retail sales and events, still showed a productive $13.4 million increase despite one fewer home game.

The bottom line: The operating numbers aren't typical of those the Packers normally see, but they aren't setting off any alarm bells within 1265 Lombardi Ave.

"The NFL is more competitive and more expensive than ever," Chairman of the Board, President and CEO Ed Policy said. "We want to ensure our football leadership has every tool in the toolbox to build a competitive roster, and we do."

The Packers demonstrated that in August when General Manager Brian Gutekunst seized a once-in-a-blue-moon opportunity to acquire Micah Parsons, a Hall of Fame-caliber edge rusher who then made an immediate impact.

This is just one example of the cost of doing business in the current hypercompetitive NFL.

The national gains in non-operating income were primarily driven by the NFL's strategic transaction with Disney, which involved the sale of the NFL Network and certain media assets to ESPN, and in return received an equity interest in ESPN which was shared equally among all 32 clubs. Ultimately, setting aside all the anomalies reflected in this latest financial report, the Packers are confident in how the broader picture looks.

"The franchise remains in great shape," Policy said. "In the short and medium term, there are no major financial concerns, and we will continue to do what it takes to compete as the NFL landscape changes and evolves, which includes being intentional on generating more local revenue.

"We are however, keeping a very close eye on current trends and how they may impact our long-term financial health."

Those trends relate to the challenges the Packers may face in keeping up financially with the rest of the league's clubs, which have access to capital via private equity and limited partners purchasing small, non-controlling stakes in teams.

"It's like other teams have an ATM that we don't have," Policy said, referring to private equity.

As the league's only publicly owned franchise, the Packers don't have access to such capital, and their roughly once-per-decade stock sales raise a small fraction compared to others' private equity offerings.

Other teams also have significant public money invested in their redeveloped or new stadiums, which allows them to spend more money on non-capped football operations.

From the Packers' perspective, Lambeau Field – which will soon be the league's oldest stadium – will need considerable investment for continued maintenance, as well as future improvements to remain a cutting-edge facility.

"It's critical to have a long-term plan in conjunction with the city, county, state, and stadium district board to keep Lambeau Field both iconic and state-of-the-art," said Policy.

Certainty is needed with the city and stadium district with respect to Lambeau's lease, and a collaborative approach will be required with the county and state for additional future plans.

The Packers do have their corporate reserve fund, which now sits at $701 million, $77 million more than a year ago thanks to a combination of investment gains and new contributions. It remains an important, strategic asset the franchise must use responsibly.

But again, comparatively speaking, that amount has taken more than 30 years for the Packers to save, while other clubs can now raise just as much in a matter of months.

Two other pieces to the franchise's financial picture include the Titletown development and the team's community impact, which are partially connected.

The organization views Titletown, in which the Packers have led a total investment of roughly $300 million from all parties involved, as a community asset that welcomed nearly a million visitors over the past year.

text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan suffered non-life-threatening injuries, including a concussion, in a car accident earlier this month, the team said in a statement.

The statement said Shanahan will participate in team activities on a limited basis at the start of training camp.

According to a Palo Alto police report, the accident occurred at 6:13 p.m. on July 14 at the intersection of Alma Street and Hamilton Avenue in Palo Alto when Shanahan collided with an SUV, resulting in fractures to the head coach’s nose, ribs and hand. He was taken by ambulance to a local hospital; the driver of the SUV was not injured. No one has been cited in the collision and drugs and alcohol are not believed to be involved, according to the police report.

General manager John Lynch on Saturday said the 49ers would treat Shanahan’s concussion as if he’s a player who suffered one.

“Kyle basically is going to be in the protocol,” Lynch said. “We’re going to let the condition, the doctors dictate how he comes back, when he comes back.”

The accident occurred before coaches and rookies reported for training camp later that week. Shanahan mostly has been working from home, though he’s recently made brief trips to the team facility.

Shanahan’s longtime assistant Chris Foerster, whose title is assistant head coach/offensive line, will run training camp with an assist from defensive coordinator Raheem Morris and others. The 49ers’ veterans report for training camp Saturday and the first practice is scheduled for Sunday.

Lynch said Shanahan might be on the field at times during training camp but that Foerster and others will handle the practices.

“We’re not going to blink,” Lynch said. “We feel like we’re well-equipped for something like this.”

This story will be updated.

title: Explaining NFL roster designations: What PUP, IR, NFI mean | Big Blue View
description:
The New York Giants recently placed three players on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list in advance of training camp.
Players must be placed on the PUP list before the beginning of training camp.
There are two varieties of PUP lists: Active PUP — These are players placed on the PUP list before training camp.
Injured Reserve (IR) Players are placed on Injured Reserve (IR) when they suffer a football-related injury that will force them to miss several games, allowing their team to replace them on the roster.
The NFI list functions similarly to the PUP list in terms of active and reserve NFI.
text:
The New York Giants recently placed three players on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list in advance of training camp. What do all of the lists/roster designations we commonly hear about mean?

Physically Unable to Perform (PUP)

The physically unable to perform (PUP) list is for players who are judged physically unable to perform in football activities due to an injury suffered playing or practicing football. Players on the PUP list can be around the team, but cannot practice. Players must be placed on the PUP list before the beginning of training camp. There are two varieties of PUP lists:

Active PUP — These are players placed on the PUP list before training camp. They are counted as part of a team’s 90-man roster, but are not allowed to practice until physically cleared and removed from PUP. A player on Active PUP can be removed from the list at any point in training camp.

Reserve PUP — If a player on Active PUP during training camp is not removed from the list, he can be placed on this list when teams cut their rosters to the 53-man regular-season limit. A player on this list must miss at least the first four games of the season. One change to this rule for 2026 is that players on Reserve PUP can now begin practicing after missing the first two weeks. Previously, the 21-day practice window to decided whether to activate a player or place him on season-ending Injured Reserve opened after the four-week time frame.

Injured Reserve (IR)

Players are placed on Injured Reserve (IR) when they suffer a football-related injury that will force them to miss several games, allowing their team to replace them on the roster.

NFL rules now allow up to two players who were placed on IR to be designated to return during the season. If a player is placed on IR before roster cutdowns, they are ineligible to return. That is why the Giants, who believe there is a small chance defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris can return this season from his torn Achilles tendon, have not placed Robertson-Harris on IR. Team can designate as many as eight players to return from IR during the season, 10 if they reach the playoffs.

Players on IR must miss at least four games.

The Non-Football Injury (NFI) list pertains to players who were injured or became ill while away from football activities, such as if they were injured working out on their own away from the team facility.

The NFI list functions similarly to the PUP list in terms of active and reserve NFI.

Kent is an official tree city, but I wish the park system would plant more trees along the hike and bike trails. I'm will be planting an oak tree in my back yard (one of my many projects).

PEACE

I wasn't born to follow.

I'm speaking as someone who has had to make the bottom line of a business end up in the right spot for quite a few years (I was briefly in charge of a $2 billion corporation through a quirk of fates, but that's another story). I can tell you that having an owner with extremely deep pockets, like 31 of the 32 teams have, is incredibly valuable. I'm certainly not a multi-billionaire, but I know enough to appreciate the value of those who are.

I was pretty young at the time, but I have a decent recollection of the events of the Indians in the 1970's. For a time (I believe it was in the Nick Mileti era) the Indians had a whole bunch of owners, with Mileti at the helm but no one with the bank account to carry the team through rough times. Nearly all those people needed for the team to at least break even so they didn't have to keep pumping cash into the franchise. That creates an extremely unstable situation. Again, I could be wrong, but I believe it was Steve O'Neill who finally came in, bought out all the hundreds of owners, and gave the franchise some stability.

I love the Packers as my second-favorite team. I lived in Madison, WI for 10 years. But the Packers' ownership model definitely has its limitations.

text:
Few positions in professional sports demand as much physical sacrifice for as brief a glimpse of glory as the NFL running back. One year, you’re the engine powering a playoff contender; the next, a single lingering injury can quietly bring the curtain down on a Pro Bowl career.

That harsh reality hit home once again following reports that former Houston Texans and Cincinnati Bengals star Joe Mixon has privately told former teammates he believes his NFL career is over.

Advertisement

For a player who spent nearly a decade imposing his will on defense after defense, seeing Mixon’s football journey end not with a triumphant final game, but in the quiet void of injury rehabilitation, is a sobering reminder of football's unforgiving nature.

A Career Reborn in Houston

To appreciate how abrupt this potential ending feels, you have to rewind to 2024. After seven productive seasons in Cincinnati, where he established himself as a focal point of the Bengals' offense and a fan favorite, Mixon was traded to the Houston Texans.

Many questioned how much gas the veteran back had left in the tank. Mixon answered those doubts immediately with one of the most complete and energized seasons of his career:

Advertisement

Rushing Production: 1,016 yards and 11 touchdowns on 245 carries.

Versatility: 36 receptions for 309 yards and an additional receiving touchdown.

Accolades: Earned his second career Pro Bowl nod while leading Houston’s ground attack to a postseason berth.

Mixon didn't just fit into Houston's offense—he galvanized it. His violent, decisive running style gave young quarterback C.J. Stroud a reliable safety net and restored Mixon’s reputation as one of the game's top feature backs.

The Foot Injury That Changed Everything

What made Mixon’s downfall so jarring was how quickly the tide turned. Following his standout 2024 campaign, high expectations for a repeat performance in 2025 were completely derailed before the season even got underway.

A severe foot injury that was compounded by complex recovery setbacks, circulatory complications, and multiple surgeries, kept Mixon off the field for the entirety of the 2025 season.

Advertisement

The Texans placed Mixon on the Non-Football Injury (NFI) list, where he remained as the months dragged on without progress. By March 2026, with the team forced to restructure its backfield, Houston granted Mixon his release.

While there was faint hope that free agency might yield a fresh start elsewhere, the quiet market and ongoing health hurdles proved insurmountable. Recent reports indicating Mixon has conceded his playing days are done feel like the final, inevitable chapter in a long, difficult ordeal.

The Unforgiving Lifespan of the Modern Running Back

Mixon’s situation isn't an isolated tragedy; it’s the structural standard of the modern NFL. The running back position has become a meat grinder. Teams routinely churn through talented ball-carriers, hesitant to hand out long-term security knowing that a back's body can break down almost overnight.

Advertisement

Selected in the second round of the 2017 NFL Draft by the Cincinnati Bengals, Joe Mixon has built one of the NFL's most productive careers as a running back. A two-time Pro Bowler (2021 and 2024), Mixon has rushed for more than 7,400 career yards while establishing himself as a consistent offensive playmaker. He has accounted for 74 total touchdowns throughout his career, including 60 rushing touchdowns and 14 receiving touchdowns, highlighting his impact as both a runner and a pass catcher.

When a back turns 29 or 30, the margin for error disappears entirely. For Mixon, a freak health setback at age 29 ended up being a hurdle too steep to clear, effectively closing the book on an otherwise stellar decade-long run.

A Legacy Worth Celebrating

If this is indeed the end of the road for Joe Mixon, sports fans shouldn't let his frustrating final year obscure what was an undeniably impressive career.

Advertisement

He leaves behind a reputation as a fierce, high-energy competitor who stepped up whenever his teams needed him most. From powering Cincinnati to a Super Bowl appearance to rejuvenating Houston’s offense, Mixon gave everything to the game.

It’s a bittersweet finish, but in a league where longevity is rare and second chances are rarer, Joe Mixon ran as hard and as far as he possibly could.

title: Barcelona players dominated Spain's World Cup-winning squad. This is why that influence ...
description:
Barcelona’s influence in this Spain team is undeniable.
Eight players in Luis de la Fuente’s squad play for the Catalans — only three World Cup-winning teams have ever had more players from a single club.
But beyond those figures, Spain’s footballing style is what truly illustrates the Barcelona influence on the world and European champions.
“Barcelona’s aim is not to feed the core of Spain’s national team,” a La Masia source, who wished to remain anonymous to protect his position, told The Athletic.
It did not impact Madrid’s success — they have won six Champions League titles since 2014 — but their influence on the national team has receded.
text:
This World Cup win heralds a new golden era for Spanish football — one that follows a similar pattern to what made the national team world beaters the first time they lifted the trophy in 2010.

Barcelona’s influence in this Spain team is undeniable. Eight players in Luis de la Fuente’s squad play for the Catalans — only three World Cup-winning teams have ever had more players from a single club. It was the most since the nine players Penarol contributed to Uruguay’s winning side in 1950.

Two of the team’s main stars, the 19-year-olds Lamine Yamal and Pau Cubarsi, came through the club’s famed La Masia academy together. Two other players on the pitch for Sunday’s final at MetLife Stadium were formed there: Argentina captain Lionel Messi and Spain left-back Marc Cucurella (who has just signed for fierce rivals Real Madrid). Ferran Torres, the winning goalscorer, came through at Valencia but has played for Barca since 2021.

The numbers are outstanding and there is sure to be more to come, with players such as Fermin Lopez — who missed this tournament through injury — and Marc Bernal tipped to be national-team regulars for the next generation.

But beyond those figures, Spain’s footballing style is what truly illustrates the Barcelona influence on the world and European champions.

“Barcelona’s aim is not to feed the core of Spain’s national team,” a La Masia source, who wished to remain anonymous to protect his position, told The Athletic. “We want to feed our first team with players that learn our philosophy by heart. But a couple of things have taken place to make this happen naturally.

“Spain adopted a new style over the last few decades that is similar to our idea. And then, we at Barca have had a tendency to ease youngsters into the first team very organically. The club trust the academy, the managers do as well and young players get real chances in the first team. It is a simple thing, but it does not happen at every club in Spain.”

Until 20 years ago, the Spanish national team identified themselves as “La Furia Española” (‘The Spanish Fury’). It embodied the style Spain wanted to play — tough-tackling, with fast and lively transitional football.

Luis Aragones changed that after his appointment as Spain coach in 2004. He decided the team needed to be based around a different type of player given the quality at his disposal. He left out the country’s most popular player, Real Madrid captain Raul in 2008, and made Barcelona midfielder Xavi the conductor of his fluid and possession-oriented style. Xavi was surrounded with equally technical and skilful players such as Andres Iniesta, Cesc Fabregas and David Silva.

That decision to go from La Furia to tiny technicians produced instant success, as Spain won the 2008 European Championship and followed it up with that World Cup win two years later, along with the 2012 Euros (the latter two were won under Aragones’ successor Vicente del Bosque, who had previously managed Real Madrid and their youth teams). When Spain lifted the World Cup in 2010, they did so with seven players from Barcelona, more than any other side.

It appeared to have an impact on Real Madrid’s transfer policy. Their president, Florentino Perez, has long been known for his preference for galactico signings from abroad, such as Luis Figo, David Beckham and Ronaldo Nazario in his first spell in charge from 2000-2006 and stars such as Cristiano Ronaldo and Kaka in his second from 2009.

After the triumph of Spain’s golden generation, Perez and Madrid spent significant funds on the most promising prospects in Spanish football. From 2013 to 2018, they signed players such as Isco, Asier Illarramendi, Marco Asensio, Jesus Vallejo, Alvaro Odriozola and Dani Ceballos — all of whom had played a big role in Spain’s youth setup.

But most of those players were unable to establish themselves at the top of the game with Madrid or flourish within the national team’s style. It did not impact Madrid’s success — they have won six Champions League titles since 2014 — but their influence on the national team has receded. The squad announced for this summer’s World Cup did not feature a single Real Madrid player for the first time (Cucurella’s move was made official midway through).

That is not for a lack of Spanish talent. Dean Huijsen and Alvaro Carreras are both Madrid players who have featured for La Roja — in Carreras’ case at under-21 level — but they have yet to find the platform to truly shine at Madrid. It has been a different story for Barca’s Spanish youngsters.

Barca’s financial struggles in recent years may well have helped players such as Yamal and Cubarsi be quickly elevated to the first team. The same is true of Bernal, Fermin, Marc Casado and Gerard Martin, all of whom have played for Spain’s senior side or the under-21s in recent years.

It is hard to envisage so many La Masia prospects playing for the first team if they had the capacity to afford more high-end signings, but it has worked out extremely well for them — and Spain can only benefit.

text:
Kansas City Chiefs coach Andy Reid addressed the media to kick off 2026 NFL training camp at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, Missouri, on Friday. Big Red provided several notable injury updates on key players.

Patrick Mahomes is fully cleared to participate in training camp practices, which is the biggest news. However, Chiefs fans also received updates on defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott, wide receiver Rashee Rice, first-round cornerback Mansoor Delane, and others as rookies, quarterbacks, and injured players reported to camp.

Omarr Norman-Lott expected to start 2026 training camp on active PUP list

Chiefs second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott will most likely start on the Active/PUP list, according to Reid. This comes after Norman-Lott suffered an ACL injury during the 2025 NFL season.

“As far as any of the injuries go right now, some updates would be Omar Norman-Lott most likely will start on PUP but is making progress,” Reid said. “He had ACL reconstruction there.”

The Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list is designated for players who are unable to pass the conditioning test at the beginning of camp. Players on the Active/PUP list still occupy a spot on the 90-man offseason roster. They can be activated at any time during training camp. If Norman-Lott remains on the PUP list through 53-man roster cuts, Kansas City would then move him to the Reserve/PUP list, requiring him to miss the first several weeks of the 2026 NFL season.

This was expected for a player of Norman-Lott’s size. Defensive tackles and offensive linemen tend to have longer recovery periods for knee ligament injuries because the injury simply takes longer to fully heal under the weight of such a big body. It is possible that Norman-Lott will be activated at some point during training camp, but the team is clearly taking every necessary precaution.

Chiefs WR Rashee Rice cleared for full participation

Reid confirmed that wide receiver Rashee Rice, who had offseason surgery to remove debris from his surgically repaired knee, is cleared to participate in full.

“Rashee Rice with his knee debridement is doing great,” Reid said. “So he will again go. We’ll keep an eye on him, but he’s cleared to go.”

Rice has had an eventful offseason between his off-the-field situation and the knee. Now, it’s time to fully focus on football and training camp. He can get himself healthy and ready for the 2026 NFL season.

2 Chiefs cornerbacks also dealing with injuries

Reid had updates on two of the team’s cornerbacks, starting with first-round draft pick Mansoor Delane. Delane suffered a shoulder injury during OTAs and sat out of mandatory minicamp.

“Delane right now is having his final physical, so he’s right in the process of that,” Reid said. “But is doing well there.”

As of now, it’s unclear if Delane will be cleared to participate in practice or if he’ll end up on the Active/PUP list. Reid’s tone seemed to track with his earlier anticipation that Delane would be healthy and ready to go, but that has not yet been confirmed.

Reid also spoke about cornerback L’Jarius Sneed, who returned to Kansas City this offseason. It seems Sneed is picking up right where he left off with the Chiefs. He dealt with a long-term knee issue the team has consistently monitored.

“And then LJ Sneed, you know, we always, like we did before, kept an eye on him with his knee, and we’ll just take him slowly and gradually, get him back into the mix there as we go,” Reid said. “But look forward to getting him on the field.”

Expect some veteran rest days for the cornerback as he gets back into the swing of things.

Undrafted free agent TE John Michael Gyllenborg unlikely to participate in training camp

Reid spoke about TE John Michael Gyllenborg, a Kansas City local who signed with the team after the 2026 NFL Draft. Gyllenborg did not participate in practices late in mandatory minicamp, and Reid confirmed a knee injury is the reason.

“Gyllenborg, he’s still working through the knee sprain which he had,” Reid said. “They’re doing some other evaluations on him, so we’ll just see for this camp here. Most likely he won’t get much work there.”

It sounds as if Gyllenborg could end up as the team’s mystery IR stash for the 2026 offseason.

As for other injury concerns, the picture will become clearer when veterans report to camp next Tuesday. As things currently stand, the Chiefs look relatively healthy heading into 2026 training camp, which is a good sign. The challenge, as always, is maintaining that same level of health throughout training camp and the preseason. Injuries are a part of football, and there will surely be others to pop up throughout the next several weeks.

description:

text:
ST. JOSEPH, Mo. — Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes has been fully cleared to participate in practice, the latest step in his return from a torn left ACL and LCL suffered in December.

As the team welcomed quarterbacks and rookies to training camp at Missouri Western on Friday, coach Andy Reid told reporters Mahomes has the all clear to “do all the different periods that we have in this camp. He’s been cleared to participate fully.”

“We’ll just take it day-by-day and see how he does,” Reid said. “He’ll have plenty of eyes on him, from coaches to trainers to doctors.”

Mahomes said Friday that he’d received the official go-ahead to return fully after meeting with Dr. Dan Cooper, who performed his December surgery.

“It was always the goal to be able to practice when we got to training camp, and so we’ve hit that next step,” Mahomes told reporters. “Now it’s just gonna be about building and keep getting better and better, so that whenever the regular season comes around, I can try to be available and ready to play.”

Mahomes has made remarkable strides since having that surgery in December — he even participated during most of the team’s May and June practices. He did non-contact work during those spring drills (while wearing a heavy knee brace) but was held out of 11-on-11s as a precaution. He told reporters in late May that running and cutting would be the next milestones as he worked his way back.

Both of those areas — running and cutting — have improved in the last few months, Mahomes said.

“That’s stuff I had to prove to the doctors and to the coaches and everybody like that to be at this point,” Mahomes said. “It’s a long process. The process isn’t over. It’ll be something I’ll probably deal with for the next few years of my career and throughout the rest of my career. But you have to stay on top of that stuff.”

As Mahomes worked his way back, Reid said he didn’t intend to treat him any differently during this training camp. But Reid said he’ll continually evaluate whether anything needs to change with his star quarterback in drills.

And as for Mahomes potentially being ready for the Chiefs’ season opener against Denver on Sept. 14? Reid wasn’t ruling out the possibility.

“I’m optimistic, and I know he is extremely optimistic,” Reid said of a Week 1 return. “But I think you’ve got to see how things go here. Let’s just see where we’re at and not make any predictions or anything else. Take it day by day, and see where it goes.”

Mahomes said the most difficult part of his rehab was early, when his knee was so bad after surgery that he wasn’t able to get on the ground and play with his children. When he was able to develop to the point he could do that, it only provided extra motivation to attack that particular day’s goals with recovery.

The 10th-year quarterback made clear, however, that Friday’s practice clearance wasn’t the finish line with this process.

“You’ve got to continue to work and get better and better, and go throughout practice and prove to the coaches, prove to the doctors and everybody that I’m the same quarterback I was before, if not better,” Mahomes said. “And I can go out there and take care of myself and win football games.”

There are ways, Mahomes says, that he feels even better than before his injury. Constant weight training in the offseason has made him feel stronger than before, and now the biggest key will be getting comfortable again with all the quarterback-specific movements he has to make.

“I feel like I wasn’t playing my best football at the end of last year before I got hurt,” Mahomes said. “And so I’ve got to find ways to get better, navigating the pocket, running the offense better and getting the ball into my hands and letting other guys make plays. And so I think this injury helped me focus on those little things as I kind of get back to being who I am.”

Mahomes said he consulted a few NFL players with past ACL injuries for advice throughout the process. That included Hall of Fame quarterback Tom Brady, former Chiefs teammate Tyrann Mathieu and longtime NFL tight end Zach Ertz, who suffered an ACL injury one week before Mahomes in December. Mahomes said he’d even had competitions with Ertz to see who was progressing the best in rehab during these offseason months.

For now? Mahomes said he expects Reid to manage training camp practice just as he would any other season.

“I don’t think he’s going to take it light on anybody, including me,” Mahomes said. “And then I’m gonna go out there and see what I can do.”

text:
We’re back with another round of dynasty-related questions, pulled from the Fantasy Life Community Discord—which I encourage you to join—and the beautiful birdies over at Bluesky.

This week, we explore the long-term values of two very popular rookies, the difference between a couple of receivers coming back from injuries, how to breathe a little life into a long-running league and SO MUCH MORE.

Let’s get into it…

By registering or logging in, you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Dynasty Fantasy Football Mailbag

What WRs do you like/hate in the BTJ/Zay Flowers/Marvin Harrison range of guys?

First of all, thank you for not phrasing your question as “Love/Hate,” as that belongs to the big boss and I’d never want to infringe on that.

The range of receivers you’re talking about is a high-upside group that’s also viewed with a healthy amount of skepticism. You could addLadd McConkey, Luther Burden and Jameson Williams to that list.

Out of this cadre, Zay Flowers feels like the sturdiest in terms of dynasty value. Not only has he performed like a versatile, top-tier receiver in back-to-back seasons—which isn’t something I can say about anyone else in that group—but Flowers has led the Ravens in targets, receptions and receiving yards every year he’s been in the league. And now there’s a decent chance the passing game improves (or at least becomes more aggressive) under new OC Declan Doyle.

The guy I simply can’t get on board with in this range is Luther Burden, who’s probably valued the highest in dynasty leagues right now. Heck, that’s partly WHY I’m not on board. Burden’s best stretch coincided with Rome Odunze’s injury. He had just as many games with NEGATIVE receiving yards as he did games with 70+ receiving yards. The Bears offense benefitted greatly from a turnover-heavy defense and some fourth quarter theatrics that are tough to bank on. I need to see more before I’m willing to pay that price for Burden.

In a rookie dynasty draft: Jadarian Price vs Jordyn Tyson.

It’s been awhile since my last rookie mock draft, but I'm still firmly in favor of Jordyn Tyson over Jadarian Price. And it doesn’t matter if you’re a contender or not.

I appreciate Price's upside, especially while Zach Charbonnet is out of office (so to speak). But we're mostly just HOPING he can step out of Jeremiyah Love's shadow and into a workhorse role with the Seahawks. The floor feels pretty nice in the short term, which makes for a compelling case in redraft, but Tyson has a significantly higher ceiling in dynasty. We’re talking cathedral ceiling. If he hits it, you’re going to be set for a long time.

I was offered Garrett Wilson for Parker Washington and a 2027 projected late first-round pick. Do I pull the trigger?

This is normally the type of question I’d save for the Rate My Trade series, but I’m powerless against any mention of Garrett Wilson.

Getting Wilson for that price is a steal in my book. And I really like Parker Washington! But there are so many more question marks around the depth chart in Jacksonville than there are at the Meadowlands.

I hate that I have to keep saying this, but I’ll do it until the world finally agrees: Garrett Wilson is arguably the most underrated receiver in fantasy football. A very smart and handsome young man even predicted in the Fantasy Life Magazine (available at a newsstand near you!) that Wilson will finish this year as a Top-8 WR:

“One could argue that Geno Smith is exactly what the fifth-year wide receiver needs right now: a consistent, veteran QB who’d rather sling the ball than scramble.”

What is your valuation on Christian Watson? If I move Rome Odunze, I might go after Watson to backfill with a cheaper option with equivalent upside.

There’s been a lot of questions about Odunze lately (and rightfully so), but Christian Watson is the perfect comparison to help explain my thoughts. Both of these guys have/had injury concerns. They’re both in similar territories as far as target trees are concerned. They could both be their respective team’s WR1, are competing with elite tight ends to be the No. 1 overall pass catcher and have exciting young WRs nipping at their heels.

The difference is how their respective injuries affect your lineups. When Watson is on the field, the odds of a big stat line are pretty high. And if the injury bug comes for him again, he goes to your bench. It’s simple.

But with Rome Odunze, the concern is how his recent injury will affect his on-field performance. Will you feel comfortable starting him without knowing what his “new normal” looks like? His spot in your lineup seems more precarious

How should a commissioner handle a long dormant trade offer being accepted after BREAKING NEWS (i.e. a player gets arrested/injured/retires)?

I’m reminded of Andrew Luck’s sudden retirement, and the shockwaves it sent through fantasy leagues when it happened. I heard story after story of long-pending trades that were suddenly smash accepted. I hate that.

It’s why I love that the Sleeper platform has an option to set a time limit on your trade offers. But ultimately, that’s an issue for team managers, not the commissioner. Do I personally think it’s extremely dishonorable and dick-ish behavior? Yes. And the manager who runs to click accept would have an enemy for life. But it’s also the responsibility of the person sending trade offers to keep track of these things and withdraw trades that have been steeping for too long.

I need to cut five guys from my roster. My options are below. Which three should I keep?

Tahj Brooks, Justice Hill, Phil Mafah, Ben Sinnott, Brandon Aiyuk, Darius Slayton, Brashard Smith, Audric Estime.

A few days ago I was mentally paralyzed by a decision I had to make that, frankly, didn't deserve as much brain power as I was giving it. I was really fretting over a pretty inconsequential thing. In the midst of all my brooding, an extremely distressing event occurred in my neighborhood that completely reset my perspective. It reminded me of all the many more important things that deserve my time and attention.

I’m very grateful for this submission because it gives me an opportunity to say this, not just to the person asking the question but to everyone reading: Follow your heart. Do what feels right. And have fun with it!

By “it” I don’t just mean this roster decision. I don’t even necessarily mean fantasy football. Take a minute to appreciate that this is something you and I get to ponder together. We get to spend parts of our days discussing the merits of Justice Hill. I think that’s a wonderful thing, but let this also be a reminder not to take it so seriously. And to make sure that we’re giving adequate energy to the things in our lives that really matter and that make a difference for others.

Thanks for letting me get that off my chest. I appreciate you all for spending part of your days with me.

text:
Everyone is chasing the Los Angeles Dodgers, even when it comes to the names they can bandy about before the Aug. 3 trade deadline. They can do anything, and don’t need to do anything.

That gives the Dodgers the freedom to be creative. The Athletic has reported that the Dodgers have discussed the idea of prospect-for-prospect trades even as their major-league roster continues to pile up wins. If the Dodgers add a major piece during this transaction period, they have plenty of prospect depth to come out of it without denting a strong farm system.

The core of the Dodgers’ system is their glut of outfielders. One of them is already out the door this deadline period, as the Dodgers traded their third-round pick from a year ago, Landyn Vidourek, to the Colorado Rockies as part of a package for reliever Seth Halvorsen.

More outfielders could be moved or used to supplement the roster. So it makes sense to check in on how some of the bigger names at the position are doing. Each grouping is broken up by level.

If these outfield prospects were included in Keith Law’s updated top 70, that ranking will be indicated. This is a non-comprehensive list; the Dodgers’ outfield depth extends beyond this group.

All numbers are accurate entering July 23.

Triple A

James Tibbs III (No. 46)

Tibbs, along with Zach Ehrhard (more on him in a bit), were among the biggest coups of last year’s trade deadline. The Dodgers acquired Tibbs, a 2024 first-round pick, from the Red Sox for Dustin May, who went on to make just six appearances for Boston.

Tibbs had an electric start to this season but slowed down when he played through a forearm injury that limited him to designated hitter duty. Still, he’s been one of the most dynamic hitters in the minors this season in his first taste of Triple A. Through his first 416 plate appearances, he’s hit .290/.411/.548 with a 143 wRC+.

A 16.6 percent walk rate is nothing to sneeze at, mixing that patient approach with enough pop to seemingly give him a strong offensive floor. The lefty has been pretty platoon-neutral this season (.976 OPS in 131 plate appearances against lefties).

He’s probably the most major-league ready player among the guys who have yet to debut, though there are still some swing-and-miss concerns (72 percent contact rate this year at Triple A).

Ryan Ward

Ward made his long-awaited debut in April and got some run with the big-league club while Teoscar Hernández was on the injured list with a hamstring strain. His 60 plate appearances are still a small sample, but he had some challenges hitting fastballs. Among hitters with that much playing time, Ward’s 40.6 whiff rate on four-seam fastballs was sixth-highest.

He’s been a producer in the minors nonetheless. His overall production is down from 2025 (notably with a drop in slugging percentage from .557 to .462), and at 28 years old he is much older than some of the other names on this list. But for clubs looking for immediate production in left field, first base or as a designated hitter, Ward could hold value.

Zach Ehrhard

It’s tough to sneeze at what Ehrhard has done at 23 years old in his first taste of Triple A. He’s hit .286 with a .393 on-base percentage and .485 slugging percentage, good for a 126 wRC+. His best production has come over the last 28 days, with a 1.058 OPS over that span. There are bat-to-ball skills, solid swing decisions and an overall intriguing package to go with the fact that he can play all three outfield spots.

Double A

Josue De Paula (No. 18)

De Paula might have the biggest name of this group after winning Futures Game MVP honors in 2025. He might have the highest offensive ceiling as well. It looks like he’s taken a real step forward in 2026, not just with his advanced approach (he’s walked 56 times in 409 plate appearances and struck out just 55) but with his batted-ball data.

De Paula is pulling the ball more (44.8 percent, up from 40.7 percent) and hitting it on the ground less (39.9 percent, down from 41.9 percent), and his power production is coming along. He’s already hit more home runs (16) than he hit all of last year (12). While the major question remains his defense, De Paula’s bat solves a ton of questions and makes it difficult to see the Dodgers moving him.

Mike Sirota (No. 17)

Sirota has stayed on the field after injuries in 2025 and has always produced when healthy. This year, it’s been 382 plate appearances of a .324 batting average, a .474 on-base percentage (and an on-base streak that lasted 72 games) and a .564 slugging percentage.

Sirota makes good swing decisions, hits for enough power to take advantage of them and could potentially stick in center field. Together, that creates one of the better prospects in baseball. The Dodgers got Sirota from the Cincinnati Reds (along with the draft pick that became Chuck Davalan) for Gavin Lux.

Zyhir Hope (No. 26)

Stick with me here. Hope has upped his contact rate from 68.3 percent last year to 74.1 percent and already has more home runs (21) than he did a year ago (13). He’s stolen 17 bases.

Hope could stand to make better swing decisions, but he continues to check the boxes in front of him. He’s tapped into more of the skills that made him so projectable when the Dodgers acquired him in another prospect challenge trade — Michael Busch and Yency Almonte to the Cubs in 2024 for Hope and Jackson Ferris. It’s a bit repetitive, but it’s another really nice season for one of these Dodgers outfielders.

Kendall George

George swiped 100 bags a year ago and has 34 stolen bases this season. He’s back in game action after a freak injury in which he hurt his knee trying to avoid a bat dog, and has stolen eight bases in the 14 official games he’s played in since returning.

It’s good to see the speed appears unaffected, because the injury overshadowed some of the real strides he was making offensively. The bat-to-ball skills are there, but he’s traded some fly balls for line drives (his fly ball rate is down from 20.6 percent to 13.1 percent), which is better for his overall skill set. George still needs to improve defensively despite his extreme speed, but that 80-grade speed is a carrying trait that separates him.

High A

Eduardo Quintero (No. 15)

Quintero is just 20 years old, but his upside is immense because of his offensive toolkit and the potential to play center field after being signed as a catcher. That would make it difficult for the Dodgers to part with him. He’s hit .294 this season with eight home runs, 35 stolen bases and a 133 wRC+ even after struggling out of the gates in April (.586 OPS through his first 95 plate appearances). Each month since has been better than the last.

He’s patient (15.9 percent walk rate), puts the bat on the ball and is already starting to hit for some power. It’s hard to ask for more at that age.

Chuck Davalan (No. 63)

The Dodgers used the competitive balance round pick they got for Lux on Davalan, believing he could stick in center field while using his athleticism and bat-to-ball skills to be a productive offensive player. Davalan has been just that in his first year in pro ball, with a 127 wRC+ in 374 plate appearances while walking more often (12.8 percent) than he’s striking out (11.2 percent). He has 14 home runs and has been pulling the ball in the air a ton. Davalan is also running an 84.9 percent contact rate, for good measure.

It would be interesting to see how his production changes once he makes it to Double A, though the glut of outfielders the Dodgers already have at the level (see above) leaves him a little blocked at the moment.

text:
Roughly half of the NFL has reported to training camp, with the last teams reporting as late as Tuesday. Over the next few weeks, news will continue to pop up, injuries will happen and teams will start working toward Week 1. Here are some big takeaways from the teams that have already reported to camp over the last couple of weeks.

Jaelan Phillips is already more valuable than his contract for the Carolina Panthers

The Carolina Panthers have been aggressive in addressing their pass rush over the last two offseasons. In the 2025 NFL Draft, the Panthers drafted Nic Scourton and Princely Umanmielen and then this past offseason, they landed Jaelan Phillips in a big free agency move. That turns out to be an invaluable move after Nic Scourton suffered a torn ACL injury on the first day of the Panthers' training camp and is now on the injured reserve list.

Advertisement

Carolina is coming off a playoff appearance last year and made the necessary moves to build toward being a playoff contender. The loss of Scourton is huge for this defense. Scourton was the lead pass rusher with five sacks. Umanmielen had just 1.5 sacks in 16 games played. That obviously means Phillips has a lot more pressure to be the top pass rusher on this team. I don't think the Panthers need to make any drastic moves to add depth, but Phillips is now one of their most important additions this offseason.

This also gives Umanmielen a chane at having a better second season. As long as Phillips is healthy, he should be good enough to give the Panthers a confident pass rush, but no playoff contender is good with just one good pass rusher, they also need a complimentary one. If nothing more, this should give Carolina a chance to find some depth on the defensive line.

New York Giants finally get positive Malik Nabers news

No NFL team has been slammed with injuries like the New York Giants this early in the preseason period. During mandatory camp, the Giants lost two defensive lineman to injuries. Finally they get some good injury news. Malik Nabers isn't getting put on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list, meaning he's on track to start Week 1. Nabers suffered a torn ACL injury last season. The Giants finally needed some good news and now maybe a little optimism for the 2026 season.

Advertisement

There's been a lot of questions around whether Nabers would be ready for the season opener and this is a step in the right direction. Of course, we'll see how he handles training camp and the preseason, but the Giants can worry a little bit less about Nabers' recovery. This is good considering Cam Skattebo's failed backflip went viral after he's in recovery for a major leg injury from last season as well.

Jacoby Brissett comes back down to earth after possible contract holdout

Jacoby Brissett reported to the Arizona Cardinals training camp and it means he's finally come back down to earth after a possible contract holdout loomed over the Cardinals. Brissett realized he wasn't going to get the money he wanted and that missing the season wasn't worth it. This is honestly the best-case scenario for all sides. Not that the Cardinals need Brissett to play, but the way he played last year, it's better to have him rather than relying strictly on Carson Beck in his first season.

Advertisement

Brissett held out voluntary workouts, seeking a pay raise, but did report to mandatory camp. With him reporting to training camp, it seems he has come to terms with not getting a pay raise for now. The two sides could still talk through options, but he's not going to let that affect his standing for the season. Not much changes for the Cardinals now other than having their full team in for training camp.

The quarterback position wasn't really a huge cause of concern, as they're using bridge options this year in hopes of landing their future franchise star in the 2027 NFL Draft.

Advertisement

Lamar Jackson has a lot to prove in pivotal 2026 season

Lamar Jackson was ranked the No. 2 player in the NFL by NFL.com last season. This offseason, he was ranked the No. 69 player. That's a massive drop-off for one of the most explosive players in the NFL. There's been a lot of criticism on Jackson and how he hasn't won an AFC title game or reached the Super Bowl. This season is as important as ever to make that happen, especially considering his contract situation.

Jackson and the Ravens are still at odds on a new contract and this year would go a long way to getting that done. If Jackson can turn regular season success into a playoff run, he can essentially ask for whatever he wants. This season, there are no more excuses as to why the Ravens can't compete for a Super Bowl. Not to say that he shouldn't get an extension, but the better he plays, the more leverage he can get. The Ravens reported to training camp on Friday meaning he's truly on the clock now.

text:
Patrick Mahomes Injury Update (Imagn Images)

Patrick Mahomes is back on the practice field. Seven months after tearing his ACL and LCL against the Los Angeles Chargers in December, the Chiefs quarterback has been cleared to practice ahead of training camp. Head coach Andy Reid confirmed the news on Friday, the team's official opening day, telling reporters he is "optimistic" Mahomes will be ready for Week 1. For a franchise coming off its worst season in years, the timing could not be better.

Is Patrick Mahomes fully recovered from his ACL injury?

The short answer, based on everything coming out of Kansas City, is that he is as close to full as anyone could reasonably expect at this stage. Patrick Mahomes underwent surgery in December and has been working through rehab ever since. The reports have been consistently positive throughout the offseason, and Friday's clearance to practice is the clearest signal yet that his body has responded well. What makes this update notable is the speed of it. Seven months from ACL surgery to practicing with your NFL team is not something every quarterback pulls off clean. Reid's optimism about Week 1 is not just coachspeak either. The Chiefs open the season on Monday Night Football against the Denver Broncos, the defending AFC West champions. That is a marquee matchup with genuine stakes, and having Justin Fields under centre instead of Mahomes would take significant shine off it. The fact that Reid is projecting confidence publicly, with camp just getting underway, says a lot. Mahomes officially hits the field when practices open to the public on Saturday at Missouri Western State University. That is not a small thing. Seeing him move, throw, and operate in a live setting will tell the football world far more than any injury report.

What does this mean for the Chiefs' 2026 season outlook?

Kansas City had a rough 2025. The offense was inconsistent, Patrick Mahomes finished as a fantasy QB11, his worst ranking since becoming a starter, and the team missed the playoffs entirely. Travis Kelce is heading toward retirement. The pressure coming into 2026 is real. But the front office has moved aggressively. Kenneth Walker III, Super Bowl LX MVP, arrives to give the run game a genuine threat it lacked last season. Defenses that load the box against Walker will leave windows open for Mahomes in play-action, and that is where he has historically been most dangerous. Eric Bieniemy is also back as offensive coordinator, the same person who helped build five consecutive top-five passing offenses with Mahomes running the show. The infrastructure around him looks stronger than it did a year ago. If Mahomes comes through training camp clean and builds rhythm heading into September, a bounce-back season is not just possible, it is the logical expectation. He has done it before under pressure. The only real variable right now is how his knee holds up through the grind of a full camp. Reid's optimism is a start. The practice field will be the proof.

text:
The Kansas City Chiefs will have their star quarterback ready to go when they open up training camp practices next week.

Mahomes has been cleared to participate in practice as he continues his recovery from the torn ACL and LCL he suffered against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 15 last season, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid told reporters on Friday.

It has been an aggressive recovery for Mahomes. The star quarterback opted to have surgery immediately after suffering the injury, helping speed up his timetable to where he is today.

The 2025 season was a difficult campaign for Kansas City. The Chiefs missed the playoffs for the first time since 2014 after being eliminated with that Week 15 loss to the Chargers. At the time, Mahomes’ chances of being available for Week 1 against the Denver Broncos looked bleak.

Kansas City is now looking to rebuild around Mahomes, who signed a new extension a little more than a month ago that keeps him under contract through 2033.

Tight end Travis Kelce is still around, bringing veteran leadership and remaining Mahomes’ security blanket. The Chiefs also added Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III, who can help balance the offensive load as Kansas City looks to ease Mahomes back into the NFL season.

Mahomes threw for 3,587 yards, 22 touchdowns and 11 interceptions in 14 games before suffering the season-ending injury last season.

text:
Will Grier isn’t staying away from football for long. Less than two weeks after announcing his retirement from the NFL, the former Florida and West Virginia quarterback is returning to the game in a new role.

According to ESPN’s Todd Archer, Grier is joining the Dallas Cowboys coaching staff as an offensive assistant. Archer added that Grier had considered taking a coaching position with the Cowboys earlier this offseason, before ultimately signing with the Carolina Panthers ahead of the NFL Draft.

The move marks a quick transition from player to coach for the 31-year-old, who officially retired from professional football on July 15.

“Former QB Will Grier is joining the Cowboys coaching staff as an offensive assistant, according to a source,” Archer reported. “Grier retired on July 15 after signing with Carolina before the draft. Before joining the Panthers he contemplated joining the Cowboys coaching staff earlier in offseason.”

Alas, Grier is no stranger to Dallas. He spent multiple seasons with the Cowboys organization between 2021 and 2024, serving primarily as a backup quarterback and practice squad member before returning to Carolina this spring.

Just weeks ago, the Panthers announced Grier’s retirement after he rejoined the franchise that originally selected him in the third round of the 2019 NFL Draft. Although his NFL playing career never developed the way many expected, Grier’s college career featured plenty of memorable moments.

He began at Florida, where he burst onto the scene during the 2015 season. Grier helped lead the Gators to a 6-0 start, highlighted by a victory over then-No. 3 Ole Miss. However, his time in Gainesville came to an abrupt halt after he received a one-year NCAA suspension following a positive test for performance-enhancing drugs.

Grier transferred to West Virginia the following spring and sat out the 2016 season under NCAA transfer rules before becoming one of the nation’s most productive quarterbacks.

Over two seasons as the Mountaineers’ starter, Grier threw for 7,354 yards and 71 touchdowns while tossing just 20 interceptions. His play under then-head coach Dana Holgorsen elevated him into the NFL Draft conversation, ultimately leading to Carolina selecting him with the No. 100 overall pick in 2019.

His professional career included stops with six organizations, including the Panthers, Cowboys, Bengals, Patriots, Chargers and Eagles. Grier appeared in just two regular-season NFL games, both coming during his rookie season in Carolina, where he completed 28 of 52 passes for 228 yards with four interceptions.

While his playing career was brief, Grier now begins a new chapter on the coaching side. The Cowboys will benefit from having someone familiar with their offensive system and quarterback room, while Grier gets an opportunity to begin building a coaching résumé at just 31 years old.

After spending years learning from multiple NFL organizations as a player, he’ll now look to apply those experiences from the sideline as he starts his next football journey in Dallas.

text:
During training camp in 2024, BJ Ojulariwas one of the main headlines: First for showing flashes as a pass rusher, then for sustaining a devastating ACL injury.

Ojulari is in the spotlight again two years later, but this time, the topic is about if he can return to that form.

"Most definitely," Ojulari said when asked if he believes the outside world is forgetting about the type of player he was expected to become. "A lot of people, they focus on what's on the field, so that's very understandable. My job is to get back out there and remind everybody who I am."

It's a mission that the 2023 second-rounder has been eager to attack. Ojulari played in eight games last year and recorded eight tackles and one sack. But he was never fully himself, so much so that even GM Monti Ossenfort noted it this offseason. His production dipped hard, far from a rookie season when he had 40 tackles, five tackles for loss, and four sacks.

It wasn't a complete shock, given the catastrophic nature of his injuries. But entering the second day of this year's training camp, he can feel that health is on his side.

"Definitely the way my body reacts," Ojulari said. "The way my knee reacts, the way I move on the field, my comfort, and most of all, it's a mental thing. Getting over that mental hurdle initially and then when I go out there, I don't have to think. Previously, I had to think about it and worry about how I feel. Now I can just go, warm up, and let it rip."

Ojulari is in the same conversation as Marvin Harrison Jr. and Darius Robinson as players who need to improve in order for the Cardinals to win. No new investments were made in the Cardinals outside linebacker room, and despite a change at head coach, defensive coordinator Nick Rallis and outside linebackers coach Matt Feeney remain.

The team finished tied for 28th in the league with 30 sacks. As much as Ojulari's potential was a factor, there's hope that 2025 third-round pick Jordan Burch can also take a jump.

"I see a lot of guys who are hungry and they want to get it," Ojulari said. "(Josh Sweat) is the main guy and he's going to be able to set the tone for us, but I see a lot of guys that can step in the first group, second group, and third group. They can play all three downs and be able to add to our depth and to our versatility."

Finding someone to compliment and play opposite of Sweat is critical. There's no shortage of opportunities, especially considering Sweat started camp on the PUP list. Coach Mike LaFleur said he is not worried about Sweat in terms of his health.

"Everybody has been on the same page the entire time," LaFleur said.

Sweat, as a leader in the room and someone who has gone through his own knee battles, has been a resource for Ojulari as he returns from the injury. While Sweat isn't on the practice field yet, Ojulari is, and that's been an encouraging sight.

"When you've been hurt so much, it's a very humbling experience," Ojulari said. "When you are able to participate and be out there and not look from the sidelines, I just come in every day with a smile on my face. I'm blessed."

text:
Patrick Mahomes has reached an important milestone in his recovery from a torn ACL and LCL in his left knee as the Kansas City Chiefs prepare to open their training camp.

Andy Reid told reporters on Friday, July 24 that Mahomes is "doing great" and has been cleared to participate in the team's practice sessions ahead of the 2026 NFL season.

"Right now, he's got clearance to practice and do all the different periods we have in this camp," Reid said of Mahomes. "We'll just take it day by day and see how he does. He'll have plenty of eyes on him from coaches to trainers to doctors, but right now, he's been cleared to go ahead and participate fully."

Reid went on to praise how Mahomes had attacked his rehabilitation during the 2026 NFL offseason, noting the team appreciated his efforts to return to the field quickly.

"He's been working so hard you have a pretty good feel that he's in a good place," Reid said.

That has led Reid to believe that this year's training camp won't be too different for Mahomes even as he continues his recovery from the injury.

That has left the 68-year-old coach feeling good about the prospect of Mahomes playing in Week 1, though Reid wouldn't definitively commit to that being the case.

"I'm optimistic, and I know he is extremely optimistic," Reid said of Mahomes playing in Week 1. "But I think you gotta see how things go here. Let's just see where we're at and not make any predictions or anything else. Take it day-by-day and see where it goes."

Patrick Mahomes provides injury update

Mahomes held his own media availability just after Reid and also addressed his injury. The veteran quarterback said he had been cleared to practice "like two days ago" and expressed excitement about his return.

Mahomes particularly emphasized how important it was for him to get on the field for the first day of training camp as he looks to gain confidence playing on his injured knee.

"I didn't wanna have to get only a couple weeks of practice in and then have to go play in a game," the veteran quarterback said. "I wanted to build it up."

Mahomes noted that he is feeling "stronger than I've ever felt" but seemed particularly concerned about getting back into the rhythm of playing quarterback on his injured knee. He was particularly critical of his performance in the games before the injury, opining he wasn't doing a good job of navigating the pocket and getting the ball to his playmakers quickly enough.

"I think this injury helped me kinda focus on those little things as I kinda get back to being who I am," he said.

Mahomes will work on getting back into rhythm over the course of Kansas City's training camp. He declined to provide insight about whether he would play in the preseason, expressing he would wait and see what the team decides as his recovery progreses.

The 30-year-old also confirmed to reporters he would wear a knee brace as he mans the position, though he noted that could change and the team is not mandating he do so.

"I will start with it on just because I feel like still I can move and be myself with it," Mahomes said. "I played with it in college, and then we'll just see where we go from there."

4:45pm: Team and player are moving closer to a rookie-scale deal, per the Boston Globe’s Ben Volin, but haggling over guarantees and an injury waiver has transpired. No. 54 overall pick Eli Stowers received $7.28MM of his $8.89MM rookie deal guaranteed, while No. 56 selection Nate Boerkircher came in at $6.74MM in guarantees. That establishes the guarantee range for Jacas, though the injury component has complicated matters.

2:02pm: The Patriots placed one of their top pass rushers, outside linebacker Harold Landry, on the active/physically unable to perform list on Tuesday. Landry is continuing to deal with a knee injury that bothered him last year, and the Patriots’ OLB group is also going into training without Gabe Jacas.

A second-round pick from Illinois, Jacas underwent cleanup surgery on his knee sometime after April’s draft. Jacas, the 55th overall selection, still has not signed his rookie contract a couple months later. He and Rams first-round quarterback Ty Simpson are the only 2026 draftees without deals.

Because he doesn’t have a contract, Jacas has not reported to camp this week. He is already well behind after not participating in rookie minicamp or attending mandatory minicamp.

Asked about Jacas on Friday, head coach Mike Vrabel said contract talks have been “positive, obviously between the club and his representative” (via Mike Reiss of ESPN). Vrabel declined to put a timeline on a potential agreement, but he has spoken with Jacas and is “positive” the two sides will work through the “contractual issues” that are keeping him away from the team.

In regards to Jacas’ health, Vrabel stated: “I can only go by what he says. And so when he gets here, we’ll evaluate that. Of course, be as smart as we can; just to see, because we haven’t seen him with us. But I would say, use the words ‘cautiously optimistic.’ But again, those conversations have been great and excited to see where he’s at.”

Jacas’ recent health issues have not been limited to his knee. A hamstring injury prevented Jacas from participating at the Combine in February or Illinois’ pro day in March. There are also concerns that a labral tear in Jacas’ shoulder could require medical attention down the line.

New England has held off on adding a free agent edge defender in recent weeks, though plans may change depending on how things shake out with Landry and/or Jacas. The Patriots won 14 games and advanced to Super Bowl LX last season, but they did despite a lackluster pass rush that ranked 19th in win rate and 26th in sacks. They arguably have not done enough to upgrade the area in the past few months.

Landry led last year’s AFC champions with 8.5 sacks, but second-place finisher K’Lavon Chaisson (7.5) left for the Commanders in free agency. The Patriots replaced Chaisson with Dre’Mont Jones (seven sacks in 2025), whom they picked up on a three-year, $39.5MM contract. Jacas was their other noteworthy pass-rushing investment in the offseason, and it remains in question whether he will contribute at all as a rookie.

text:
ST. JOSEPH, Mo. -- As he has done throughout his rehab, Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes achieved the next checkmark in his return from his left knee injury when he wanted, just two days before his Friday arrival at Missouri Western State's campus for the team's training camp.

The Chiefs' medical staff and Dr. Dan Cooper, the Dallas Cowboys' head team physician who performed the surgery to repair the torn ACL and LCL in the quarterback's left knee, cleared Mahomes on Wednesday to fully participate in camp.

"I feel stronger than I've ever felt, as far as strength and lifting [weights]," Mahomes said Friday. "I feel amazing. ... I'm excited just to be able to play football. I've been seeing cinderblock walls rehabbing every single day in Kansas City. Now, to be on that practice field with my teammates, it's going to be a lot of fun."

Just as he did during the Chiefs' offseason program, Mahomes said he'll continue wearing a compression sleeve and a brace on his left leg. The big difference from two months ago is that Mahomes is expected to lead the first-team offense during team periods -- 11-on-11 repetitions -- throughout camp. Earlier this week, Mahomes showed the medical staff that he can run, cut and change directions to demonstrate that he can protect himself around his teammates.

Coach Andy Reid said he doesn't plan on limiting Mahomes from his usual repetitions. For the first time since his injury in December, Mahomes will go through repetitions alongside his top skill position players -- running back Kenneth Walker III, tight end Travis Kelce and receivers Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy and Tyquan Thornton.

"He's been working so hard that you have a pretty good feel that he's in a good place," Reid said of Mahomes. "We've got to see how things go and not make any predictions about [Week 1]."

Throughout his recovery, Mahomes has made it his mission to be the starter for the Chiefs' season opener, a home game Sept. 14 against the Denver Broncos on "Monday Night Football." Mahomes plans to use the camp practices to show the medical staff, the coaching staff and his teammates that he can be the same quarterback -- or an even better one -- that he was prior to his injury. His plan is to improve his movement within the pocket, sharpen his decision-making skills and throw the ball quicker than he did at times last season.

"I don't get hit, so that's one part of it, but it's good to be out there and have bodies around and be able to go through and run the offense," Mahomes said. "I want [Coach Reid] to call [plays] it like we're going to call it in the regular season. That's going to be the best way for me to prepare myself. I want to go out there and test [the knee]."

If Mahomes continues to progress well, the Chiefs will have to decide if he will play in one of the first two preseason games to further prepare for Week 1. Throughout his nine-year career, Mahomes has never missed the entire preseason.

"I'm a competitor, so [on] game day I'm going to want to be out there," he said. "But I understand the process of getting myself ready to play in the regular season is more important. We'll see. The coaches and doctors will make that decision for me, but I'll prepare myself like I'm going to play."

In preparing for a pivotal camp, Mahomes shared that he was given advice and encouragement from two former star players in legendary quarterback Tom Brady and safety Tyrann Mathieu, both of whom continued their All-Pro careers after sustaining a torn ACL.

"The process isn't over," Mahomes said. "It'll be something I'll probably be dealing with the next few years of my career, and throughout the rest of my career. But I feel comfortable now being able to go out there and run the offense the way the offense is supposed to be run.

"This will be the hardest training camp that you can have, as far as preparing for the season. I'm glad I'm able to do that, starting tomorrow."

title: Agent's Take: Brandon Aiyuk has only himself to blame for 49ers limbo chaos - CBS Sports
description:
The San Francisco 49ers report to training camp this weekend, and wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk is still under contract.
"I will not be reinstating with [the 49ers] nor doing any kind of business with them," Aiyuk said via 49ers Web Zone recently.
Voided guarantees and the 49ers' leverage The 49ers voided the $27 million in 2026 salary guarantees late last July in the four-year, $120 million contract extension Aiyuk signed at the end of August 2024.
Aiyuk blamed his former agent, Athletes First's Ryan Williams, for his problems with the 49ers during the latter part of June.
